The GrowthCred field guide

You work eight hours. You get paid for 2.4.

You didn't go to law school to chase invoices at 10pm. Or to rebuild your timesheet on a Friday afternoon, trying to remember what you did on Tuesday. But that's the job now, isn't it? Here's where the money goes. And how you get it back.

By Phila Ngwenya · Published 28 September 2026

Your week, honestly

Let me describe your week. You run the firm. You also take the intake calls. You review the draft invoices. You chase the client who hasn't paid since June. And somewhere in there, you're meant to be the rainmaker who brings in new work.

Then Friday comes. You sit down to capture your time. What did you do on Tuesday? You scroll your email. You check your calendar. You guess. Some of it never makes the timesheet at all.

Every owner I sit down with has a version of this week. The law isn't the hard part. Running the firm is. And it's eating you alive.

The number that should keep you up at night

Clio tracks billing data from thousands of law firms. Here's what its 2025 Legal Trends Report found. In an eight-hour day, the average lawyer records 3.0 billable hours. They invoice 2.6. They collect 2.4.

Read that again. Eight hours in. 2.4 hours paid.

Now look at collections. Firms collect 93% of what they invoice. Sounds close, right? Say your firm invoices R50 million a year. That's R3.5 million you did the work for and never got paid. Not because your clients are bad. Because the invoice went out late. Because nobody followed up. Because it sat in someone's inbox for three weeks.

And that's only the work you invoiced. Firms bill 88% of the time they record. So every R100 of work you capture turns into about R82 in the bank. The other R18 just leaks.

Then there's the wait. The median firm takes 43 days to bill its work. Then another 32 days to get paid. That's 75 days between doing the work and seeing the money. You're financing your clients. Interest free.

One caveat, because you're a lawyer and you'd ask. Clio's data comes mostly from North American firms. So pull your own numbers from your practice system. Then see if yours look any better.

Admin eats your most expensive hours

The admin isn't just annoying. It's expensive. 8am surveyed 400 legal professionals for its 2026 Admin Misery Index. 39% lose four or more productive hours a week to admin. 63% work outside normal hours. And 22% admitted they'd missed a deadline because of admin.

A missed deadline. Because of admin. In a law firm.

Your hour as a partner is the most expensive hour in the building. When you spend it formatting an invoice, the firm pays partner rates for clerk work. That's like paying your gardener and then mowing the lawn yourself.

Why hiring doesn't fix it

So you hire. What does a junior associate cost you a year? Add a practice manager. Add an admin person. Write the total down. That's your bill. Every year. Before you've managed a single one of them.

And they still need you. The invoice still waits for your review. The tricky intake still lands on your desk. People take leave. Someone resigns in February. Then you're back where you started, plus a recruitment fee.

Doing it yourself? You're already doing it yourself. That's the problem.

Buying more software? Now you've got a new login and the same Friday afternoon. Software stores the work. It doesn't do it.

The fix: write your firm down once

Here's what I do instead. I start by writing down how your firm actually runs. Your intake questions. Your fee structures. Your engagement letter precedents. When invoices go out. How you chase. What a good client update sounds like. That's the foundation of the Command Core.

Then AI does the preparation the way you would. It drafts the day's time entries from your calendar and your documents. You approve them in minutes. It drafts the invoice when a matter hits its billing stage. It sends the polite reminder on the due date. It collects the intake facts before the first call. It prepares the proposal from your approved precedents.

What it connects to depends on the systems you already use. We check that before we promise anything. But the principle doesn't change. You stop doing the work. You start approving it.

Faster: same day, not 75 days

So why does this beat every other option? Three reasons. Faster, cheaper, no risk.

Faster first. Right now a proposal takes days. Intake takes hours per client. Your money takes 75 days to arrive. Those are the numbers I build against.

The targets are simple. Proposals out the same day you meet the client. Invoices out the week the work is done. Intake finished before the first call. We measure where you start, so you'll know exactly what moved.

And it's not months of consulting. The first systems go in on day one. The full build takes 90 days. You see the first result within 14 days.

Cheaper: one system, not three salaries

Remember that salary total you wrote down? That's what you're really comparing against. Every year. And it still needs managing.

The Command Core does the preparation those hires would do. It doesn't take leave. It doesn't resign in February. It never forgets your fee structure.

You get a quote after we've scoped your firm. Before you commit to anything. Put it next to your salary total. If hiring wins, hire. If we're not a fit, we'll tell you.

No risk: 20% of your week back, or you don't pay

A lot of consultants want half the money upfront. Before they've shown you anything. You're not even sure it'll work, and they want a deposit.

Here's my deal. If the Command Core doesn't give you back at least 20% of your week, the engagement is on us.

So let me say it again. Faster than hiring. Cheaper than hiring. And if it doesn't work, you don't pay. Faster, cheaper, no risk.

What stays with you

One thing doesn't change. You're the lawyer. The system prepares. You decide.

It doesn't do legal research. It doesn't give advice. It doesn't file anything or touch the trust account. A practitioner checks every authority, deadline and client commitment before it goes anywhere. Why so strict? The Legal Practice Council's 2026 ethics guide deals with South African cases where AI invented the authorities.

Your client data follows rules you approve. We agree the tools, the access and the retention before any real matter goes near it.

Who am I to tell you this? I've given seven AI talks at WeWork Johannesburg. I co-developed an AI system presented at Parliament. I've built five companies with AI. I won't show you a law-firm case study, because I haven't published one yet. That's exactly why the guarantee exists.

Faster, cheaper, no risk. You don't have to be convinced. You just have to look at the 7% you never collect, and ask how long you want to leave it on the table. You practise law. We handle the rest.

Frequently asked questions

How much billing does a law firm lose?+
Clio's 2025 Legal Trends Report found the average firm invoices 88% of the time it records and collects 93% of what it invoices. That's about R82 in the bank for every R100 of work recorded. The data is mostly North American, so check your own numbers.
Can AI do legal work for my firm?+
Not the legal judgement. The system prepares time entries, invoices, reminders, intake packs and draft proposals. A practitioner checks every authority, deadline and client commitment. We don't offer legal research or advice.
How fast does it work?+
The first systems go in on day one. The full build takes 90 days, and you see the first result within 14 days. We measure where you start, so you'll know what moved.
